name: Track hotel rate position against a comp set with Bright Data, GPT-5.6, Google Sheets and Slack

parameters.content:
## See what your comp set is charging on the dates you have not priced yet

Rate shopping is an hour in a browser that is stale two days later. This runs it every Monday across four future dates, and says where you are priced out of the band.

### How it works

**`Build The Date Grid`** turns the horizons in Settings into four Google Hotels searches - same market, same guest count, four different check-in dates. All four go to Bright Data as one job, so there is one snapshot to poll rather than four.

Each row carries `booking_options`: every channel selling that property, with its own price. Two things happen before any arithmetic. **Sponsored rows are dropped** - the six cheapest options on the one real hotel in testing were all ads. And anything outside your star band goes, because a market search puts vacation rentals next to hotels and averaging them means nothing.

What is left gives, per date: the comp set's median and quartiles, your own cheapest rate, your rank, and the spread across channels on your own listing. GPT-5.6 writes the note; the numbers are computed in code, not by the model.

### Setup

1. Bright Data, as a Header Auth credential. The free tier is 5,000 credits a month with no card.

2. An OpenAI credential, a Google Sheet and a Slack credential.

3. In **Settings**: `property_name` roughly as Google lists it, `market_search_term` as you would type it into Google Hotels, `nights_ahead` as a pipe-separated list of horizons. `accommodation_type` is a case-sensitive enum - `Hotels` works, `hotels` is rejected.

4. Paste your Sheet URL into **`Save The Rate Grid`**. One row per date per run.

## 1. Four dates, one job
Google Flights rejects a date field outright. Google Hotels requires three, which is the only reason a rate grid is possible at all.

## 2. Ask once, not four times
The Web Scraper API takes an array of inputs, so the whole grid is one snapshot. Four separate jobs would be four poll loops on this canvas.

## 3. Wait, but not forever
One search input took 288 seconds in testing. The poll cap lives in the Code node, because a Wait has no idea how many times it has run.

## 4. Drop the ads, then do the arithmetic
The six cheapest booking options on the one real hotel in testing were all sponsored. Ranking on the raw minimum argues for cutting a rate you should hold.

## 5. The model writes, the code counts
Every number in the note was computed above. The model is given them and told not to invent others, and not to name a new rate.

## 6. One row per date, one message per run
Without the Split Out the sheet gets a single row whose columns are `message` and `rows`. Without executeOnce, Slack gets the digest four times.

## These are published rates, not your rates

Everything here comes from what Google Hotels shows a member of the public on one day, in one country, in one currency. It is not your PMS, it does not know your negotiated corporate rates, your allotments, your length-of-stay rules or what is already on the books. A comp set that looks cheap may be selling a non-refundable rate against your flexible one.

**Do not wire this to anything that changes a price.** It ends in a spreadsheet and a Slack message on purpose. Rate decisions need occupancy and pace, and neither is visible from outside.

One search input took **288 seconds** in testing. Four dates on one job is a slow run by design - leave the poll cap alone unless you have watched one finish.

parameters.text:
=You are writing the rate note a revenue manager reads on a Monday morning. Every number below was computed from live Google Hotels data; do not invent any others and do not restate all of them.

Property: {{ $('Settings').first().json.property_name }}
Market: {{ $('Build The Date Grid').first().json.market }}
Stay length: {{ $('Build The Date Grid').first().json.stay_nights }} night(s)

Per date, as JSON:
{{ JSON.stringify($('Work Out Your Position').all().map(i => ({date: i.json.date, your_rate: i.json.your_rate, median: i.json.median, p25: i.json.p25, p75: i.json.p75, rank: i.json.rank, of: i.json.rank_of, comp_count: i.json.comp_count, channel_spread: i.json.channel_spread, your_cheapest_on: i.json.your_cheapest_on, your_dearest_on: i.json.your_dearest_on, found_you: i.json.found_you, top_comps: i.json.top_comps.map(c => ({hotel: c.hotel, price: c.cheapest, rating: c.rating, star: c.star})) })), null, 1) }}

Write at most four short paragraphs, no headings, no bullet list.
- Open with the one date that most deserves attention and say why in numbers.
- Say where the property sits against the quartiles, not just the median. Sitting above p75 and sitting between the median and p75 are different situations.
- If channel_spread is more than about 15% of your own rate, say which channel is selling you cheapest and which dearest, and treat it as a parity question rather than a pricing one.
- If found_you is false for a date, say plainly that the property did not appear in that search and that its numbers are missing, rather than reasoning around it.
- Name specific competitors only when their price actually supports the point.
Do not recommend a specific new rate. You cannot see occupancy, pace or what is already on the books, and a number here would be read as advice it is not.
